targetText: In 1930, after thirteen years of British occupation of Palestine, the Director of Education admitted in his report that: "Since the beginning of the occupation, the government has never undertaken to provide sufficient funds for the building of a single school in the country," and in 1935, the government turned down 41% of the applications by Palestinian Arabs for places in schools.
summary: British colonial authorities deliberately neglected public education in Arab communities to keep the rural masses illiterate and politically submissive.
explanation: British mandatory administration severely restricted educational expenditures for Arab schools, building zero government schools in over 500 villages. Keeping the rural population illiterate was a calculated colonial strategy to stifle political organization and modern technical skills.

targetText: Moreover, the government "censored books and objected to all cultural links with the Arab world, and did nothing to raise the educational level of the peasants..."50
summary: British colonial censorship severed Palestinian intellectual ties with neighboring Arab cultural centers to inhibit anti-colonial solidarity.
explanation: The mandatory power strictly banned progressive literature and periodicals from Egypt, Syria, and Iraq, seeking to isolate Palestinian youth from anti-imperialist discourse circulating throughout the Arab world.

targetText: Popular poetry in particular reflected a growing concern on the part of the rural masses over the course of events. This spontaneous awareness led to a spirit of mobilization in the villages.
summary: Oral poetry and vernacular culture served as primary mediums of anti-colonial political agitation among illiterate rural fellahin.
explanation: Because formal schooling was denied to the peasantry, folk poetry (zajal) recited at village weddings and market gatherings functioned as oral newspapers and revolutionary agitprop, articulating popular grievances against land theft and colonial violence.

targetText: The majority of urban intellectuals, for their part, were of a feudal or commercial petty-bourgeois class affiliation. Although they basically advocated a type of bourgeois revolution, the objective conditions were by no means favorable to the development of the class that would logically lead such a struggle. As political activists, they thus remained under the control of the traditional leadership.
summary: Palestinian urban intellectuals were tied to feudal and merchant interests, preventing them from leading an independent democratic revolution.
explanation: The Palestinian educated petty bourgeoisie was economically dependent upon traditional landowning families and commercial import-export houses. Lacking an independent industrial economic base, they could not break free from the hegemony of the feudal-clerical leadership.

targetText: We do not know of a single Palestinian writer or intellectual in that period who did not participate in the call for resistance against the colonial enemy. There is no doubt that the intellectuals, even though they were not, in general, mobilized by a revolutionary party, played an important role in the national struggle.
summary: Palestinian writers and poets unanimously championed anti-colonial resistance despite the absence of an organized revolutionary vanguard party.
explanation: Intellectuals such as Ibrahim Tuqan, Abd al-Rahim Mahmud, and Abu Salma placed their literary work in service of the anti-colonial resistance. However, because their efforts were not guided by a disciplined Marxist-Leninist party, their agitation remained romantic and politically vulnerable to co-optation.

targetText: Having completed their studies and returned to their towns, they became aware of the incapacity of the class they belonged to of leading the national struggle. But at the same time they suffered from their own inability to participate and benefit from the process of industrial development that was essentially controlled by an alien and hostile community.
summary: Educated youth faced structural marginalization, blocked from industrial careers monopolized by British and Zionist enterprises.
explanation: Young Palestinian graduates found themselves economically locked out of modern professions and managerial positions, which British authorities and Zionist corporations reserved for European personnel. This blocked upward mobility generated deep frustration and radicalized student youth.

summary: Progressive Palestinian intellectuals began articulating a Marxist class understanding of British colonialism rather than viewing it through communal lenses.
explanation: Pioneering Palestinian Marxist thinkers argued that imperialism was an economic system grounded in capitalist super-profits and class exploitation, rejecting simplistic religious or racial explanations and laying early foundations for anti-colonial socialist theory.

summary: Popular revolutionary poetry urged armed resistance as the only path to destroy centuries of feudal deference and colonial subjugation.
explanation: Kanafani cites this stark popular verse to illustrate how peasant culture cast off fatalistic submissiveness. In conditions of settler dispossession, armed struggle became the psychological and political vehicle for the peasantry to assert its human dignity and revolutionary agency.
